subject: Numeracy
title: Sorting and matching
objectives: Children will sort objects by colour and size.
Children will find pairs and the odd one out.
content: Sorting by colour and size, matching pairs, and finding the odd one out.
teachingActivities: Let children choose their own sorting rule at first; name the rule aloud ("these are all red"); use real objects such as bottle tops, leaves and fruit; ask "How did you sort?"; accept any sensible rule.
learnerActivities: Sort objects by colour and size, find pairs and spot the odd one out.
resources: Picture cards for odd one out
assessment: Observe whether each child sorts by colour or size and says how they sorted.
expectedOutcomes: Sorts a set of objects by colour or size.
Finds the odd one out with support.

lessons.title: Sorting by colour
lessons.subject: Numeracy
objectives: Children will sort objects by colour and say how they sorted.
successCriteria: Puts objects of one colour together
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can count objects to 10, name numerals 1 to 10 and play counting games.
resources: Bottle tops in red, blue, green and yellow
lessons.starter: Hold up a red bottle top and say "This is red. Where do the red ones go?"
teacherActivities: Show how to put red bottle tops into a red basket.
Give each child a handful of mixed bottle tops.
Let children sort them into the baskets.
learnerActivities: Children watch and name the colour.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show how to put red bottle tops into a red basket. Children: Children watch and name the colour.
Step 2. Teacher: Give each child a handful of mixed bottle tops. Children: Child looks at the colours.
Step 3. Teacher: Let children sort them into the baskets. Children: Child sorts by colour.
Step 4. Teacher: Ask "How did you sort?" Children: Child says by colour.

practical.title: Colour baskets
steps: Put colour cards on the mat.
Put it in the matching basket.
practical.safety: Use bottle tops larger than a fist or check they are not small enough to swallow. Supervise closely and keep tops out of mouths.

differentiation.support: Sort two colours only and name each colour together.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to sort by colour and then count each group.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

lessons.conclusion: Look at the full baskets and say the colours.
lessons.homeConnection: Sort socks or spoons by colour at home.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "sort objects by colour and say how they sorted" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Sorting by size
lessons.subject: Numeracy
objectives: Children will sort objects by size into big and small.
successCriteria: Puts big and small objects in groups
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can count objects to 10, name numerals 1 to 10 and play counting games.
resources: Two hoops labelled big and small
lessons.starter: Hold up a big and a small leaf and say "Which one is big? Which one is small?"
teacherActivities: Show how to sort leaves into big and small hoops.
Give each pair a bag of mixed leaves and stones.
Let children sort them into hoops.
learnerActivities: Children watch and say big or small.
Children say which hoop has more.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show how to sort leaves into big and small hoops. Children: Children watch and say big or small.
Step 2. Teacher: Give each pair a bag of mixed leaves and stones. Children: Pairs look at the objects.
Step 3. Teacher: Let children sort them into hoops. Children: Child sorts by size.
Step 4. Teacher: Check the hoops together. Children: Children say which hoop has more.

practical.title: Big and small hoops
practical.safety: Check leaves and stones are clean with no sharp edges and wash hands after. Use only large safe objects.

differentiation.support: Offer one big and one small object at a time.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to sort three sizes.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

lessons.conclusion: Wash hands and say big and small.
lessons.homeConnection: Sort spoons or shoes by size at home.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "sort objects by size into big and small" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Matching pairs
lessons.subject: Numeracy
objectives: Children will find matching pairs of objects.
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can count objects to 10, name numerals 1 to 10 and play counting games.
lessons.starter: Hold up one sock and say "Where is the other one? It must be the same."
teacherActivities: Show a sock and find its pair from a pile.
Give each child one sock to match.
learnerActivities: Child turns cards to find a pair.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show a sock and find its pair from a pile. Children: Children watch and say same.
Step 2. Teacher: Give each child one sock to match. Children: Child finds the matching sock.
Step 3. Teacher: Play the matching card game. Children: Child turns cards to find a pair.
Step 4. Teacher: Count the pairs. Children: Children count the pairs.

practical.title: Find the pair
practical.safety: Use clean items and wash hands after handling socks and shoes. Keep floors clear.

differentiation.support: Offer three items with one match.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to find pairs that are almost the same.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

lessons.conclusion: Put the pairs away and count them.
lessons.homeConnection: Match socks and shoes with your child at home.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "find matching pairs of objects" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Odd one out
lessons.subject: Numeracy
objectives: Children will find the odd one out in a group of objects.
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can count objects to 10, name numerals 1 to 10 and play counting games.
resources: Groups of four objects with one different
lessons.starter: Show three red bottle tops and one blue and say "One is different. Which one?"
teacherActivities: Show a group with one different and ask which is odd.
Let children find the odd one in other groups.
Let children make an odd one out for a friend.
learnerActivities: Children point to the odd one.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show a group with one different and ask which is odd. Children: Children point to the odd one.
Step 2. Teacher: Say why it is different. Children: Children say different colour.
Step 3. Teacher: Let children find the odd one in other groups. Children: Child points and says why.
Step 4. Teacher: Let children make an odd one out for a friend. Children: Child makes a group.

practical.title: Odd one out
practical.safety: Use large safe objects and supervise the game. Keep objects away from mouths.

differentiation.support: Use groups where the difference is a clear colour.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to find an odd one out by shape.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

questions.question: Which is the odd one out?

lessons.conclusion: Put the objects away and say well done.
lessons.homeConnection: Make an odd one out game with household objects.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "find the odd one out in a group of objects" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Week 6 sorting check
lessons.subject: Numeracy
objectives: Teachers will observe how each child sorts and matches.
successCriteria: Finds pairs and odd one out
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children can count objects to 10, name numerals 1 to 10 and play counting games.
lessons.starter: Sing the sorting song and show three stations.
teacherActivities: Set up three stations: colour sort, size sort and odd one out.
At each station ask "How did you sort?"
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Set up three stations: colour sort, size sort and odd one out. Children: Children rotate every five minutes.
Step 2. Teacher: At each station ask "How did you sort?" Children: Child answers with a word.
Step 3. Teacher: Record each child’s level. Children: Children tidy at the signal.

practical.title: Sorting stations
practical.safety: Supervise each station and use large objects only. Keep floors clear.

differentiation.support: Provide an adult partner and use two colours.
differentiation.extension: Ask a confident child to sort by two features.

assessment.method: Observe and record Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding for: sorts by colour; sorts by size; finds pairs; finds the odd one out; says the sorting rule.

expectedOutcomes: Has an observation record for Week 6
lessons.conclusion: Wave goodbye and say well done.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "Teachers will observe how each child sorts and matches" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?
